summary: Describes the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) version 1.0, a framework meant to let different electronic commerce systems interoperate. It aims to give consumers, merchants and payment providers a common way to run purchases online. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: IOTP gives online shops, banks and delivery firms a common way to run one trade together. Each side sends the same kinds of messages, and any payment system can travel inside them. The RFC covers version 1.0 only, so it is a starting point rather than a finished protocol.

questions: what are the iotp trading exchanges
what are the iotp trading roles
subtitle: A shared XML vocabulary for online trading, so a shop, a bank and a courier can run one purchase together.

tldr.problem: Online trades split into several jobs: selling, taking the payment, delivering the goods and handling complaints. Each seller, bank and courier used its own messages, so their software could not work together.
tldr.mechanism: IOTP defines XML messages built from trading blocks and trading components. It names five trading roles and four trading exchanges, and it carries a payment system's own messages inside its own messages without changing them.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes Baseline IOTP version 1.0, a small set of eight transaction types built from six document exchanges. It is an Informational memo, so it sets no Internet standard, and it leaves payment schemes and transports to separate supplements.

today: RFC 2801 was published in April 2000 as an Informational memo, so nothing in it is an Internet standard, and no later RFC has replaced or amended it. The document covers Baseline IOTP version 1.0 and points to separate supplements for each payment scheme and each transport, and RFC 2802 covers digital signatures in more detail.

sections.title: Why IOTP Exists
sections.content:
The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) sets out a common framework that lets separate e-commerce systems work together. It makes no assumption about how money moves, and it can carry payment systems such as SET, Mondex, CyberCash, DigiCash and GeldKarte inside its own messages. One framework covers every arrangement, whether the shopping site, the Payment Handler, the Delivery Handler and the customer support provider sit in one organisation or in four.

The RFC's aim is to reproduce, safely, the steps of real trade: agreeing who takes part, presenting an offer, paying, issuing a receipt, delivering the goods and receiving them. Three goals are listed: trading models people already recognise, trading models the Internet makes possible, and interoperability across the world. Two unfamiliar parties that both conform to the specification should be able to complete a business safely and successfully.

The RFC sets out what has changed between physical and online trading. Face-to-face dealing becomes the exception rather than the rule. Authentication is harder, because without a familiar face there is no shared object and no familiar dialogue to confirm who is who. The payments industry cannot economically support very small transactions, yet the Internet makes fractions of a currency worth trading. Goods can also be delivered electronically, and payment may have to be final and non-refundable while delivery still has to be confirmed first. Incremental delivery, such as listening or viewing time, is a further model that behaves differently online.

This document is Baseline IOTP, covering the trades people make most often, such as purchases and refunds. The authors expected the scope not to change while implementers worked, only to be corrected where problems were found. Software had already been built against earlier revisions, including version 0.9 published in early 1998. The RFC says it does not prescribe the software each participant must build, and it does not address legal or regulatory issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Two companies that have never met should be able to buy and sell safely over the Internet, just as they do in a shop. IOTP is the shared set of messages that makes that possible, whatever payment system each side prefers.

sections.title: The Five Trading Roles
sections.content:
IOTP talks about a trade through roles, not through company names. An organisation may hold a single role or every one of them, and a firm that sells online is the Merchant on one side of a deal and the Consumer on the other.

  • Consumer: the person or organisation that receives the goods or services and pays for them.
  • Merchant: the party a purchase is made from; it carries the legal responsibility for supplying the goods or services and collects the money.
  • Payment Handler: the body that actually takes the Consumer's money, acting for the Merchant.
  • Delivery Handler: the body that actually hands over the goods or services to the Consumer, acting for the Merchant.
  • Merchant Customer Care Provider: the body that talks through and settles customer disputes for the Merchant.

At one end a single merchant handles the purchase, accepts the payment, delivers the goods and provides customer care. At the other end a merchant handles the purchase but sends the consumer to a bank or financial institution to pay, asks an overnight courier firm to deliver, and points the consumer at an organisation that provides a 24x7 service if problems arise. Because the words name roles and not organisations, the same protocol fits every one of these arrangements.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol splits a sale into five jobs. A shop, a bank and a courier can each take one job, or the same company can take all of them. Nothing in the rules depends on which arrangement you choose.

sections.title: The Four Trading Exchanges
sections.content:
A Trading Exchange is a swap of data between two roles. IOTP defines four of them, and every transaction is built from a combination of them.

  • Offer: the Merchant gives the Consumer the reason why the trade is taking place. The name is deliberate: no trade continues until the Consumer has accepted it.
  • Payment: a payment of some kind between the Consumer and a Payment Handler. It may run in either direction, and a refund is a payment the other way.
  • Delivery: passes either downloadable goods or the details of a physical delivery from the Delivery Handler to the Consumer.
  • Authentication: lets one role ask another to prove its identity.

In the general payment case the Merchant sends a Brand List holding the payment brands, protocols and currency amounts on offer. The Consumer answers with a Brand Selection naming the brand, protocol and amount it picked. The Merchant then returns the payment details, optionally signed, and the Consumer sends a Payment Request to the Payment Handler. The messages of the chosen payment scheme ride inside Pay Scheme Data components, and the Payment Handler closes with a Payment Response that carries a receipt. Where it saves a round trip, components belonging to different exchanges travel together in one combined message.

The Delivery Exchange finishes with a Delivery Note. It may hold customer-care details such as a shipping tracking number, or the electronic goods themselves. The Authentication Exchange has an Authenticator, which sends a challenge and a list of the algorithms that may be used, and an Authenticatee, which answers it. A Status component then carries the result.
sections.plainLanguage: Buying something online takes a few predictable steps, and IOTP pins down each one. The seller sets the terms, the buyer pays, the goods arrive, and any party can be asked to prove who it is.

sections.title: Messages, Blocks and Components
sections.content:
An IOTP message is an XML document that is well formed, and its root element is IotpMessage. Inside that root sit Trading Blocks. Each block holds a fixed set of Trading Components, which are the XML elements carrying the data for one exchange. The document type definition allows one Transaction Reference Block, then an optional Signature Block, an optional Error Block and any number of Trading Blocks. Those Trading Blocks are the Authentication Request, Authentication Response, Authentication Status, Cancel, Delivery Request, Delivery Response, Inquiry Request, Inquiry Response, Offer Response, Payment Exchange, Payment Request, Payment Response, Ping Request, Ping Response, Trading Protocol Options and TPO Selection blocks, sixteen in all.

The Transaction Reference Block identifies the transaction and the message inside it. Its TransId component carries a globally unique transaction identifier, a version, the transaction type and a timestamp, and the same TransId appears in every message of one transaction. Its MsgId component identifies the message, names the message it answers through RespIotpMsg, sets the language, and carries a SoftwareId that must name the manufacturer, the software, its version and its build. RelatedTo components tie a transaction to another one, for instance a refund that refers back to an earlier purchase.

The IotpTransType attribute names the standard transaction under way. The Baseline values are BaselineAuthentication, BaselineDeposit, BaselinePurchase, BaselineRefund, BaselineWithdrawal, BaselineValueExchange, BaselineInquiry and BaselinePing.

Trading Blocks come in three shapes. A Request Block asks for an exchange to start, an Exchange Block carries data back and forth during it, and a Response Block says the exchange is complete. The RFC leaves the transport to separate supplements, so the same messages can travel over different mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IOTP conversation travels as XML documents. Every document names its trade and its own message number up front, and the rest of the file holds the details of one step.

sections.title: Identifiers and Element References
sections.content:
Messages, blocks and components all carry an XML ID attribute. No two elements in one transaction share a value, and a value never changes once it is set, even if the element is copied into a later message. Any element can therefore name any other element in the same transaction with an Element Reference, for example to name the Payment Handler organisation a payment uses. A reference is resolved by finding the element in the same transaction whose ID matches.

A message identifier is one prefix followed by digits. The prefix is M for the Merchant or C for the Consumer, with I used for inquiry and ping requests and Q for inquiry and ping responses. For a block or a component, take that message identifier, add a dot and a number. As a guide, the second message a Consumer sends carries the identifier C2, and the first new component inside it carries C2.1. The rules are written as a grammar in the RFC:

IotpMsgId_value ::= IotpMsgIdPrefix IotpMsgIdSuffix
IotpMsgIdPrefix ::= NameChar (NameChar)*
IotpMsgIdSuffix ::= Digit (Digit)*
BlkOrCompId_value ::= IotpMsgId_value "." IdSuffix

References are typed as NMTOKEN rather than IDREF, because the element referred to is not always in the same XML document.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything inside a trade is stamped with an identifier that stays the same for the life of the trade, even when the piece is copied into a later document. A part that needs to refer to another part simply quotes its identifier.

sections.title: Extending IOTP and Packaged Content
sections.content:
The XML element and attribute names used by IOTP form an XML namespace, so extra elements can be added at any level: new Trading Blocks, new Trading Components or new elements inside a component. A new block or component must have an ID attribute of its own. IOTP keeps one attribute in reserve, IOTP:Critical, that tells a receiver how to treat an extension it cannot interpret. Set to True, it means an application that cannot process the element has a Technical Error and the transaction must fail. Set to False, the transaction may carry on, but the extra element still has to travel with its parent whenever that parent is copied, and it still has to be part of any signature digest. An extension with no such attribute is treated as True, and the value applies to all child elements too.

The Packaged Content element carries embedded data safely inside XML. Examples are payment scheme messages such as SET messages, and the description of an order, a payment note or a delivery note. Its Content attribute says what it holds: PCDATA, MIME, MIME:mimetype or XML. Its Transform attribute is NONE or BASE64, and its Name attribute distinguishes several Packaged Content elements in the same place.

Language is marked with xml:lang. A sender may list preferred languages and character sets, though the receiver is under no obligation to use them. Net locations come in a secure form, where privacy is protected by something such as SSL/TLS, and an insecure form. Either or both must be present, and where both are the sender chooses.

Any role may cancel a transaction by sending a message that carries only a Cancel Block. A Consumer should not cancel a transaction that has already completed, and cancelling a complete transaction is treated as a technical error.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put extra information into an IOTP message if you say whether a reader must understand it. If a reader cannot handle a part marked as essential, the trade stops. If it is marked as optional, the trade goes on and the part travels along untouched.

sections.title: Errors, Retries and Idempotency
sections.content:
The RFC draws a line between two kinds of failure. A technical error has nothing to do with what the message was for; malformed XML is one. It is reported in an Error Component that sits inside an Error Block. A business error belongs to the work being done, such as not enough money in the account. It is reported in the Status Component of the response block that matches. A business error never produces an Error Component.

Errors also sit at one of three depths. A transport level problem, such as no route to destination or a timeout, is always a technical error. A message level problem means the whole message is wrong, for example the XML is not well formed. A block level problem affects one block or component while the rest of the message is sound.

An Error Component carries a Severity of Warning, where the transaction can still continue, TransientError, where resending the message may fix it and MinRetrySecs gives the minimum wait, or HardError, where the transaction must stop. If one message reports several errors, act on the most serious one. Error codes include XmlNotWellFrmd, XmlNotValid, ElMissing, AttMissing, MsgBeingProc and SystemBusy, and no error code is longer than 14 characters.

A network may deliver a message twice or drop it entirely, so IOTP insists on idempotency: a request that changes something must not do it twice, which is what keeps a customer from paying for an order twice. When a server sees the same message a second time it sends back the reply it gave before, or, if the first attempt is still running, it answers with a MsgBeingProc transient error. To decide whether two messages are identical, the RFC recommends comparing a DOM hash. A server that is too busy to cope replies with the transient SystemBusy error. Because identical requests get identical replies, an inquiry or a ping that needs fresh status has to use a new message ID.

On the business side, the Status Component reports a ProcessState of NotYetStarted, InProgress, CompletedOk, Failed or ProcessError. A failed process carries a Completion Code, at most 14 characters long, naming the problem: InsuffFunds, BrandNotSupp, CurrNotSupp, InstBrandInvalid, BadInstrument, ConsCancelled and others.
sections.plainLanguage: A slow connection can deliver the same message twice, so the protocol makes each request safe to repeat. A customer who presses pay twice is charged once. Failures come in three strengths: ignorable, worth retrying, and final.

sections.title: Signatures, Privacy and Payment Security
sections.content:
Digital signatures in IOTP are entirely optional, and IOTP works successfully without them, although the RFC notes that an open network is less safe that way. Whether messages are signed is the Merchant's decision, and whether an unsigned transaction is safe enough is the Consumer's decision. The RFC gives reasons to sign: to show that a merchant can be trusted, to produce a record good enough for a purpose such as tax authorities, and to let a Payment Handler know the amount has not been tampered with. With no signature, a Consumer could change the amount owed simply by deleting a digit. It also gives reasons not to sign: roles may be combined, so changes can be spotted by comparing the data directly, and the cost of the cryptography may be too high for a payment of a few cents.

Inside a Signature Component sits a Manifest listing digests of other components, and those components may be anywhere in the same transaction and may themselves be signatures. When a Merchant signs an Offer, the result is an Offer Response signature. Later the Payment Handler signs that together with the record of the payment, producing a Payment Receipt signature. The two are then tied together, so the payment belongs to that offer. Symmetric or asymmetric cryptography may be used, and a single transaction may use both. A Consumer does not have to be given certificates. The details of how signatures are formed and checked are in RFC 2802.

Privacy comes from sending messages over a secure channel such as SSL/TLS, and that is optional too. IOTP is blind to the payment protocol inside it, so it neither helps nor hinders payment security; that belongs in the supplement for the payment protocol. What IOTP does is bind together the record of each exchange in a transaction, so that an Offer, a Payment and a Delivery can be tied to one another.
sections.plainLanguage: Sealing a message with a digital signature is a choice, not a requirement. The signature proves that nobody edited the amount on the way, but the cost of making one may not suit a payment of a few cents.

sections.title: The Baseline Transactions
sections.content:
Baseline IOTP names eight transaction types. They are assembled from six Document Exchanges: Authentication, Brand Dependent Offer, Brand Independent Offer, Payment, Delivery, and Payment with Delivery. A Document Exchange is a set of messages that does the work of one Trading Exchange or of two at the same time, which keeps the number of messages down. A Brand Dependent Offer lets the Merchant adapt the offer to the brand the Consumer picked, for instance to give a discount for using a store card; a Brand Independent Offer does not change with the choice.

  • Purchase: authentication if wanted, then an offer, then a payment, then a delivery if one is needed. A Payment and Delivery Document Exchange can combine the last two steps.
  • Refund: authentication if wanted, then an offer, then a payment running from the Merchant to the Consumer.
  • Value Exchange: two payments that shift value from one pairing of currency and payment method to a different one.
  • Deposit and Withdrawal: putting electronic cash into, or taking it out of, a financial institution.
  • Authentication: one party puts a question to another and may ask for that party's organisation details in return.
  • Inquiry: asks how a transaction is getting on, whether it is still running or already finished. It uses an Inquiry Request block and an Inquiry Response block, and inquiries about Ping transactions are ignored.
  • Ping: checks that another IOTP application is alive and able to handle signatures. Every IOTP aware application must answer a Ping Request with a Ping Response. A Ping does not affect any ongoing transaction and does not start one.

The RFC also fixes what an implementation must support to claim that it supports IOTP. The scope depends on the roles the solution covers: store merchant, electronic cash value issuer, electronic cash value acquirer, Consumer, Payment Handler and Delivery Handler. A table marks each transaction and trading block for each role as Must, May, Depends or Limited, where Depends means the requirement follows from support for the Baseline Authentication transaction or from a payment method's supplement. A solution must support all the transactions and blocks required by at least one role before it can be described as supporting IOTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight different trades are defined here, from a simple purchase to a two-payment swap of value, plus two small ones for checking on progress and on whether the other end is alive. Each trade lists which steps it must perform, and each company implements only the steps its own job requires.

sections.title: Brands, Logos and Brand Identifiers
sections.content:
Payment is the part of a trade most likely to differ between sellers, so IOTP gives it names. The means a Consumer uses to pay is called a Payment Instrument. It might be a credit card such as MasterCard or Visa, a debit card such as Maestro, a smart card holding electronic cash such as a Mondex Card or a GeldKarte card, or a software account such as CyberCoin or DigiCash. The Brand is the mark that stands for one type of payment instrument. A Merchant puts a list of brands in front of the Consumer, who picks one, and each brand can have a Payment Handler of its own.

The RFC draws two further kinds of brand. A Dual Brand lets one instrument act as though it were two brands. A Japanese UC MasterCard, for example, works as a UC card or as a regular MasterCard. The Merchant lists UC and MasterCard as two brands, and the Consumer's software picks the instrument that matches the brand chosen. A Promotional Brand gives the Consumer something extra. The benefit can arrive at the moment of purchase, as with a 5% discount when paying with a Walmart MasterCard at a Walmart site, or later from the card issuer, as with loyalty points credited when the payment appears on a statement. Each promotional brand should be listed as a separate brand so that both sides can recognise it.

Logos are fetched over the network. The full address of a logo is the logo net location, then the size, then the colour depth, then .gif. There are five standard sizes: 32 x 32 or 32 x 20 pixels (exsmall), 53 x 33 (small), 103 x 65 (medium), 180 x 114 (large) and 263 x 166 (exlarge). There are three standard colour depths: 4 bits per pixel for 16 colours, 8 bits per pixel for 256 colours and 24 bits per pixel for 16 million colours. An omitted colour depth means 256 colours.

The codes IOTP uses are registered with IANA under the procedure in RFC 2434, so that their meaning and usage stay well defined and duplicate codes are avoided. The initial Brand identifiers are Amex, Dankort, JCB, Maestro, MasterCard, NICOS, VISA, Mondex and GeldKarte. New values are announced to the IETF Trade mailing list and, if there are no objections within three weeks, allocated on a first come first served basis.
sections.plainLanguage: The brand is the name printed on the card or account, such as Visa or Mondex. A merchant lists the brands it accepts, the buyer picks one, and the protocol gives every brand a fixed identifier so both sides talk about the same one.

left.title: Technical error
left.desc: Has nothing to do with the purpose of the message, such as malformed XML. Reported in an Error Component inside an Error Block.

right.title: Business error
right.desc: Belongs to the process being carried out, such as insufficient funds. Reported in the Status Component of the matching response block.

items.label: Transaction continues
items.desc: There is a message in error, but the IOTP transaction can still continue.

items.label: Try again later
items.desc: Resending the message in error may fix it; MinRetrySecs gives the minimum wait.

items.label: Transaction stops
items.desc: There is an unrecoverable error and the IOTP transaction must stop.
